entry: Order of semiaquatic, predatory [[Reptile|reptiles]] known as crocodilians. The order appeared 83.5 million years ago in the Late [[Cretaceous]] period. Crocodilians are the closest living relatives of [[Bird|birds]], the two groups being the only known survivors of the Archosauria. The order includes the true [[Crocodile|crocodiles]] (family Crocodylidae), the [[Alligator|alligators]] and caimans (family Alligatoridae), and the [[Gharial|gharial]] and false gharial (family Gavialidae). Crocodilians are ectotherms with thick, scaly skin and a four-chambered heart. They live mainly in the warm, tropical areas of the Americas, Africa, Asia and Oceania, usually in freshwater, and are generally solitary and territorial. Some species, particularly the [[Nile crocodile]], have attacked humans. Hunting, poaching and habitat destruction are the greatest threats to crocodilian populations. Artistic and literary representations of crocodilians have appeared since at least [[Ancient Egypt]].

Type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that can affect any segment of the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]]. Symptoms often include [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], abdominal pain and [[Weight loss|weight loss]]. Its cause is unknown but is believed to involve environmental, immune and bacterial factors in genetically susceptible people; about half the risk is genetic. Tobacco smokers are three times as likely to develop it as non-smokers. There is no known cure; treatment aims to control symptoms, maintain remission and prevent relapse. About one in five people with the disease is admitted to hospital each year, and half require [[Surgery|surgery]] during the next 10 years.

Plant or plant product harvested for human use. Crops are cultivated at scale to produce food, fiber, fuel and other products. They have been central to human civilization since the first agricultural revolution, when early societies domesticated plants for food and trade. Today a small number of staple crops, such as [[Rice]], [[Wheat]], [[Maize]] and [[Sugarcane]], account for the majority of global production. As of 2004, only about 300 of an estimated 50,000 edible plant species had been domesticated as crop plants. Cropping methods include monoculture, the growing of one crop species in a field at a time, and crop rotation, the sequence of different crops grown on the same land over successive seasons. Cover crops, planted to improve soil health and reduce erosion, are grown rather than sold.

Binary operation on two [[Euclidean vector|vectors]] in three-dimensional space. The cross product of linearly independent vectors a and b, written a × b, is a vector perpendicular to both, with a direction given by the [[Right-hand rule|right-hand rule]] and a magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram the vectors span. It is zero if the vectors are parallel. The product is anticommutative and distributive over addition, and it should not be confused with the [[Dot product|dot product]]. It has applications in mathematics, physics, engineering and [[Computer programming|computer programming]], and in physics it describes quantities such as [[Torque|torque]] and [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]].

Ranged weapon using a bow-like assembly, called a prod, mounted horizontally on a frame called a tiller, which is held like the stock of a long gun. Crossbows shoot bolts or quarrels. Unlike a bow, a crossbow is spanned and cocked in advance, so the user has unlimited time to aim, and one person can operate a cocked crossbow while others reload. Mechanical devices such as cranequins and windlasses span crossbows of high draw weight, which can give greater precision and let less-trained personnel use them effectively. Reloading takes longer than with a bow. The earliest known crossbows were invented in ancient China in the first millennium BCE, and the medieval European crossbow took many of its names from [[Ballista|ballista]], an ancient Greek siege engine. Firearms have largely replaced crossbows in war, but crossbows remain used in [[Shooting sports|competitive shooting]], hunting and quiet shooting.

Word game played on a grid of black and white squares. Solvers enter words or phrases, called entries, that cross each other *across* and *down* according to numbered clues. Crosswords commonly appear in [[Newspaper|newspapers]] and [[Magazine|magazines]]. The earliest puzzles resembling the modern form were popularized by the New York World in the 1910s. Puzzles grow harder through the week in American newspapers such as [[The New York Times]], where Monday puzzles are the easiest and Saturday puzzles the hardest. A person who constructs or solves crosswords is a *cruciverbalist*, a word coined in the 1970s from [[Latin]] roots meaning *cross* and *word*.

2000 *wuxia* film directed by [[Ang Lee]]. Adapted from the Chinese novel by Wang Dulu, it follows two master warriors, Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien, after the treasured Green Destiny sword is stolen. It premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2000 and grossed $213.5 million worldwide, including $128 million in the United States, the highest-grossing foreign-produced film in American history. It received 10 [[Academy Awards]] nominations and won four, including Best Foreign Language Film.

Method of [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]] and torture in which the condemned is tied or nailed to a large wooden cross, beam or stake and left to hang until death. The process can take minutes to days; when coupled with starvation it typically takes many days, but an executioner may sever an artery while nailing the victim, causing death within minutes from blood loss. Crucifixion was used across the ancient world, including by Greece, Persia, Carthage and Rome. It remains legally sanctioned in some Muslim-majority countries and is also recorded in cases of [[Murder|murder]], [[War crime|war crimes]] and [[Genocide|genocide]]. The Roman practice is best known through the [[Crucifixion of Jesus|crucifixion of Jesus]].

Execution of [[Jesus]] by [[Crucifixion|crucifixion]] in 1st-century Judea, most likely in AD 30 or AD 33. According to the four canonical gospels, Jesus was tried before the Sanhedrin and then by [[Pontius Pilate]], who sentenced him to be scourged and crucified to satisfy a crowd or the high priests. He was crucified at Calvary (Golgotha) between two convicted thieves and, according to the Gospel of Mark, died around 3:00 p.m. Other ancient sources, including [[Josephus]] and [[Tacitus]], attest to the event. Near universal scholarly consensus holds that it occurred, though there is no consensus on its details. Jesus' suffering and death are central to [[Christianity|Christian]] doctrines of salvation and atonement.

Unmanned, self-propelled guided [[Missile|missile]] that sustains flight through aerodynamic lift for most of its path. It is designed to deliver a large warhead or payload over long distances with high precision, at high subsonic, supersonic or hypersonic speeds. In 1944 Germany deployed the first operational cruise missiles, the V-1, which used a [[Gyroscope|gyroscope]] for guidance and was accurate only against very large targets, such as the general area of a city. In the Soviet Union, [[Sergei Korolev]] headed a cruise missile project from 1932 to 1939. Postwar American and Soviet programs advanced the technology during the [[Cold War]].

Large [[Passenger ship|passenger ship]] used mainly for [[Vacation|vacationing]]. Unlike [[Ocean liner|ocean liners]], which are used for transport, cruise ships make round-trip voyages to ports of call, where passengers may go on shore excursions. As of November 2022 there were 302 cruise ships operating worldwide, with a combined capacity of 664,602 passengers. P&O introduced passenger cruising in 1844, sailing from [[Southampton]]. The industry has been criticized for its environmental impact, and large cruise ships have been identified as one of the major causes of overtourism.

Four Catholic polities, also called Outremer, established in the [[Levant]] and southeastern [[Anatolia]] from 1098 to 1291. They were the County of Edessa (1098–1150), the Principality of Antioch (1098–1268), the County of Tripoli (1102–1289) and the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]] (1099–1291), the most prominent. Their foundation followed the [[First Crusade]], proclaimed by the Latin Church in 1095 to reclaim the Holy Land. Because few settlers were Crusaders after 1130, the name is considered misleading. The [[Franks|Franks]], as Western Europeans were known, formed a largely urban minority under separate legal and religious systems. Edessa fell to the Zengid Turks in 1144. The [[Mamluk Sultanate|Mamluks]] captured Antioch in 1268 and Tripoli in 1289, and their capture of Acre in 1291 ended the Kingdom of Jerusalem, whose survivors fled to Cyprus.

Outermost solid shell of a planet, dwarf planet or natural satellite. It is usually distinguished from the underlying mantle by its chemical makeup, though on icy satellites it may be defined by its phase. The crusts of Earth, Mercury, Venus, Mars and the Moon formed by igneous processes and were later modified by erosion, impact cratering, volcanism and sedimentation. Secondary crust, formed by partial melting of mantle silicates, is usually basaltic and is the most common crust in the Solar System; on Earth it forms mainly at [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean spreading centers]]. Earth's crust is less than 1% of the planet's volume and forms the top of the [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]]. Earth has continental crust, 30–50 km thick, and oceanic crust, 5–10 km thick and denser. Earth's primary crust has not survived, because erosion and plate tectonics have destroyed rocks older than about 4 billion years.

Constellation of the southern sky, the smallest of the 88 modern constellations. It is centered on four bright stars forming a cross-shaped asterism known as the Southern Cross, and its name is Latin for cross. Its brightest star, Acrux, has an apparent magnitude of 0.8, and each of the four main stars is brighter than +2.8. The constellation lies on the southern end of the visible band of the [[Milky Way]]. It contains four [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid variables]], and the [[Dark nebula|dark nebula]] known as the Coalsack Nebula lies to its southeast. [[Ptolemy]] regarded the stars as part of [[Centaurus]].

Portions of Earth's surface where water is in solid form, including [[Sea ice|sea ice]], [[Snow|snow]], [[Glacier|glaciers]], [[Ice sheet|ice sheets]], ice on lakes and rivers, and frozen ground such as [[Permafrost|permafrost]]. The cryosphere is one of five components of the climate system, alongside the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere, and it influences climate through feedbacks on surface energy, moisture and [[Albedo|albedo]]. Most of the world's ice volume is in Antarctica, while Northern Hemisphere winter snow and ice cover the largest area, averaging 23% of hemispheric surface area in January. About 10% of Earth's surface is covered by ice, but this is rapidly decreasing. Climate change is causing measurable declines in ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover.

Digital asset that uses distributed ledger, or [[Blockchain|blockchain]], technology to enable secure transactions. Ownership records are stored in a [[Database|database]] whose consensus mechanism, usually proof of work or proof of stake, secures transaction records and verifies transfers. Despite the name, cryptocurrencies are not considered currencies in the traditional sense, and jurisdictions have classified them as commodities, securities or currencies. [[Bitcoin|Bitcoin]] was created in January 2009 by the pseudonymous developer [[Satoshi Nakamoto]]. The market has undergone several bubbles and crashes, including in 2017–2018 and 2021–2023.

Solid material with highly ordered microscopic structure. Its atoms, molecules or ions form a crystal lattice that extends in all directions, and macroscopic crystals are usually recognizable by flat faces at characteristic angles. The scientific study of crystals is [[Crystallography|crystallography]]. The word derives from the [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greek]] *krustallos*, meaning both *ice* and *rock crystal*. Examples include [[Snow|snowflakes]], [[Diamond|diamonds]] and [[Salt|table salt]]. Most inorganic solids are polycrystals, made of many microscopic crystals fused together, including most metals, rocks, ceramics and ice. Solids without periodic order, such as [[Glass|glass]], wax and many plastics, are [[Amorphous solid|amorphous]]. Despite its name, lead crystal is a type of glass rather than a crystal.

Process producing a [[Crystal|crystal]], a solid with a uniform pattern of [[Atom|atoms]] or [[Molecule|molecules]]. Crystallization can occur by precipitation from [[Solution (chemistry)|solution]], freezing of a [[Liquid|liquid]] or deposition from a gas, and its results depend on temperature, air pressure, cooling rate and solute concentration. It has two stages: nucleation, in which clusters of molecules reach a critical size and become stable nuclei, and crystal growth, in which the nuclei enlarge. Many compounds have more than one crystal structure, a property called polymorphism; [[Titanium dioxide]] has the phases anatase and rutile. In [[Chemical engineering|chemical engineering]], crystallization separates a pure solid from a solution.

Branch of science devoted to the study of molecular and crystalline structure and properties. The name derives from [[Ancient Greek]] words meaning clear ice and to write. Before the 20th century, crystals were studied by measuring the angles of their faces with a goniometer. Max von Laue performed the first [[X-ray|X-ray]] diffraction experiment in 1912, and modern methods use X-rays, neutrons or electrons. Neutron diffraction is valuable for locating light atoms such as hydrogen. Crystallography has elucidated the structures of [[Protein|proteins]] and [[Nucleic acid|nucleic acids]]; the structure of [[DNA]] was elucidated in part through X-ray diffraction studies by [[Rosalind Franklin]] and others. In 2012 the [[United Nations]] proclaimed 2014 the International Year of Crystallography.

Ancient city on the eastern bank of the [[Tigris]], about 35 km southeast of [[Baghdad]] in modern [[Iraq]]. It served as a royal capital of the [[Parthian Empire|Parthian]] and [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] empires for over 800 years and grew into a commercial metropolis that merged with the Hellenistic city of Seleucia. In the late 6th and early 7th century it was listed by some accounts as the largest city in the world. Ctesiphon fell three times to the Romans during the Roman–Parthian Wars and fell in 637 during the [[Muslim conquest of Persia]]. Afterward it declined and was depopulated by the end of the 8th century, as Baghdad became the Abbasid capital. The most conspicuous remaining structure is the Taq Kasra, once part of a royal palace and sometimes called the Arch of Ctesiphon.

Fictional cosmic entity created by writer [[H. P. Lovecraft]]. It was introduced in the short story "The Call of Cthulhu", published in *Weird Tales* in 1928, and is considered a Great Old One worshipped by [[Cult|cultists]]. It is depicted as a gigantic entity in a green humanoid form with features of an octopus and a [[Dragon|dragon]]. Cthulhu is the namesake of the Lovecraft-inspired Cthulhu Mythos and has featured in numerous pop culture references, including the [[Role-playing game|role-playing game]] *Call of Cthulhu*.

Island country in the Caribbean (pop., mid-2025: 9.8 million); capital [[Havana]]. Cuba was part of the [[Spanish Empire]] until the [[Spanish–American War]] of 1898, after which it was occupied by the United States and became independent in 1902. Following the 1959 revolution led by [[Fidel Castro]], which toppled Fulgencio Batista, Cuba became a socialist state in which the Communist Party is enshrined in the constitution. Political opposition is prohibited, and Reporters Without Borders has characterized Cuba as one of the worst countries for press freedom. Its alliance with the [[Soviet Union]] ended with that union's dissolution, after which Cuba faced a severe downturn known as the Special Period. The economy depends on tourism and on exports of skilled labor, sugar, tobacco and coffee.

13-day confrontation between the [[United States]] and the [[Soviet Union]], October 16–28, 1962. American nuclear missiles in Turkey, Italy and England were within range of Moscow, and in July 1962 [[Nikita Khrushchev]] and [[Fidel Castro]] agreed to place Soviet nuclear missiles in [[Cuba]] to deter a US invasion. After U-2 spy planes photographed the launch sites, [[John F. Kennedy]] ordered a naval blockade, which he called a *quarantine* to avoid the formal implications of war. Under an agreement, the Soviets would dismantle their offensive weapons in Cuba under [[United Nations]] verification, in exchange for a public US pledge not to invade Cuba; the United States secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey. The crisis led to the Moscow–Washington hotline and is widely considered the closest the [[Cold War]] came to full-scale nuclear war.

Military and political movement that overthrew the [[Dictatorship|dictatorship]] of Fulgencio Batista, who ruled [[Cuba]] from 1952 to 1959. It began after Batista's 1952 coup, which ended Cuba's emerging democracy. [[Fidel Castro]] and his brother Raúl led an armed assault on the Moncada Barracks on July 26, 1953, which failed, and the Castros went into exile in [[Mexico]]. They returned in 1956 with Argentine revolutionary Ernesto Guevara and fought from the Sierra Maestra, where rebels of the 26th of July Movement toppled Batista at the turn of 1958–1959. Afterward Castro's government nationalized industries and centralized the press, which, with economic problems, contributed to the Cuban Exodus to the [[United States]]. In 1965 the movement reformed along Marxist–Leninist lines as the Communist Party of Cuba. Historian Hal Brands describes Cuba as the ideological and strategic heart of [[Cold War]] Latin America.

Three-dimensional [[Polyhedron|polyhedron]] with six equal square faces, eight vertices and twelve edges of equal length. It is a special case of the cuboid and the three-dimensional member of the hypercube family, which includes the [[Square|square]] and the [[Tesseract|tesseract]]. In *Timaeus*, [[Plato]] associated the cube with the classical element of earth, and it is one of the [[Platonic solid|Platonic solids]]. The cube appears in toys, the arts, optical illusions and architecture, and in crystal structures. A cube with unit edge length is the canonical unit of [[Volume|volume]] in three-dimensional space. Its volume is a³ and its surface area is 6a², where a is the edge length.
